byTheNumbers.title: The year in numbers
byTheNumbers.standfirst: The 1930 census counted a nation of 123 million, and about four in ten homes had a radio, as the Depression began.

items.title: Population
items.summary: The 1930 census counted 123.2 million people, 16.2 percent more than in 1920 and 34.7 to the square mile.

sources.label: U.S. Census Bureau: Decennial census historical facts, 1930
Wikipedia: 1930 United States census

items.title: Radio in the home
items.summary: About 40 percent of households had at least one radio in April 1930, ranging from 63 percent of homes in New Jersey to 5 percent in Mississippi.

sources.label: National Archives, Prologue: The 1930 census
Museum of Broadcast Communications: Radio audience

items.title: Motor vehicles
items.summary: Registrations reached 26.7 million: 23.0 million cars, 3.7 million trucks and 40,500 buses.

sources.label: Historical Statistics of the United States, Table Df339-342: Motor vehicle registrations
FHWA Highway Statistics Summary to 1995, Table MV-200: Motor vehicle registrations

items.title: Out of work
items.summary: Unemployment averaged 8.9 percent in 1930; one source counts 3.2 million jobless and another 4.3 million.

sources.label: Shmoop: The Great Depression timeline
University of M'sila (Algeria) e-learning: The Great Depression

byTheNumbers.scarcityNote: Life expectancy, literacy, urban share and household size could not be confirmed for 1930 from a source we opened.

foodAndKitchen.title: Food and the kitchen
foodAndKitchen.standfirst: Bread came sliced from the store, and a year of hard times was beginning.

items.title: Sliced bread goes national
items.summary: Wonder Bread was marketing sliced bread nationwide by 1930, two years after a Missouri bakery first sold it on 7 July 1928.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Sliced bread
Smithsonian National Museum of American History: sliced bread object record

items.title: Soup kitchens
items.summary: Cities fell back on the cheapest relief, soup kitchens giving free meals to anyone who turned up, and unemployed men queued outside them in Chicago in 1931.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Great Depression in the United States

foodAndKitchen.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced 1930 grocery prices, relief meals or kitchen appliances, so only the one food change we could confirm is shown.

clothingAndStyle.title: What people wore
clothingAndStyle.standfirst: In hard times women turned feed sacks into dresses, and patches and darning kept clothes going.

items.title: Dresses from feed sacks
items.summary: Cotton feed sacks became free fabric for poor families, and women traded them; by the 1920s and 1930s manufacturers printed patterned and coloured sacks for home seamstresses.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Feed sack dress
The Saturday Evening Post: Common threads, how Depression-era women turned feed sacks into fashion
Piecework Magazine: Make do, feed sack fashion in the first half of the twentieth century

items.title: Patching and darning
items.summary: Patches, darning and other mending extended the life of clothes, and households focused on durable, practical wardrobes.

sources.label: The Saturday Evening Post: Common threads, how Depression-era women turned feed sacks into fashion
Piecework Magazine: Make do, feed sack fashion in the first half of the twentieth century

items.title: White for black
items.summary: In June 1931 Vogue observed that white had replaced black as the favoured shade for evening and formal day wear.

sources.label: Wikipedia: 1930s in Western fashion

items.title: The year of the hat
items.summary: A hat Adrian designed for Greta Garbo in the 1930 film Romance set off a nationwide buying craze, and Vogue called 1931 the Great Hat Year as tight cloches gave way to other shapes.

sources.label: Wikipedia: 1930s in Western fashion

items.title: Glamour on a budget
items.summary: Cheap but glamorous accessories such as diamanté clips, bracelets and brooches were sold to budget-conscious women through catalogues, and hemlines stayed long despite the Depression.

sources.label: Wikipedia: 1930s in Western fashion

clothingAndStyle.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced descriptions of 1930 fashion or ready-made prices.

workAndWages.title: Work and wages
workAndWages.standfirst: A manufacturing week was about 44 hours.

items.title: A factory week
items.summary: A manufacturing worker averaged 43.6 hours a week, a railroad worker 42.9 and a coal miner 33.3.

sources.label: Historical Statistics of the United States, Table Ba4589-4591: Average weekly hours in manufacturing, 1900-1957

items.title: Wages hold, then fall
items.summary: President Hoover urged businesses to keep wage rates high, and it was not until 1931 that owners began cutting wages to stay afloat.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Great Depression in the United States

workAndWages.scarcityNote: We could not find a sourced 1930 wage figure: the Historical Statistics earnings table we opened ends in 1929.

schoolAndChildhood.title: Growing up
schoolAndChildhood.standfirst: The school year had grown to about 173 days.

items.title: The school year
items.summary: The average school term was 172.7 days and a pupil attended 143.0 of them; 82.8 percent of enrolled pupils were present on a given day.

sources.label: NCES Digest of Education Statistics 2003, Table 36: school term and attendance, 1869-70 to 1999-2000

schoolAndChildhood.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced figures on enrolment, school costs or toys for 1930.

gettingAround.title: Getting around
gettingAround.standfirst: More than 26 million motor vehicles were registered, 3.7 million of them trucks.

items.title: Trucks and buses
items.summary: Besides 23 million cars, the roads carried 3.67 million trucks and 40,500 buses.

sources.label: Historical Statistics of the United States, Table Df339-342: Motor vehicle registrations

gettingAround.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced 1930 fares or journey times; the vehicle count is under The year in numbers.

keepingInTouch.title: Keeping in touch
keepingInTouch.standfirst: The family gathered in the evening to listen.

items.title: Amos 'n' Andy
items.summary: The fifteen-minute radio serial Amos 'n' Andy topped the national ratings in 1930-31 and 1931-32.

sources.label: Encyclopedia.com: 1930s TV and radio

items.title: The first daytime serial
items.summary: Painted Dreams, which premiered on WGN on 20 October 1930, is generally considered the first daytime serial drama on radio.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Golden Age of Radio

items.title: A family affair
items.summary: Radio listening was largely a family affair, mostly in the evening.

sources.label: Museum of Broadcast Communications: Radio audience

keepingInTouch.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced 1930 postage, telephone or telegraph details.

leisureAndFun.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced material on films, sport or holidays for 1930; radio is under Keeping in touch.

spotlight.title: Making do in the Depression
spotlight.standfirst: Hard times in 1930 meant fewer jobs, tighter budgets and a radio that families kept when they gave up other things.

items.title: The jobless
items.summary: Unemployment averaged about 8.9 percent in 1930, and sources count between 3.2 and 4.3 million people out of work.

sources.label: Shmoop: The Great Depression timeline

items.title: Radio before the icebox
items.summary: Social workers observed that some poor families would give up their iceboxes before they gave up their radios.

sources.label: Encyclopedia.com: 1930s TV and radio

items.title: The first banking crisis
items.summary: Rural banks began failing in October 1930 after farmers defaulted on loans, and over 800 banks had closed by January 1931.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Great Depression in the United States

items.title: Spending on clothes halves
items.summary: National spending on clothing, accessories and jewellery fell from $11.2 billion in 1929 to $5.4 billion in 1933.

sources.label: The Saturday Evening Post: Common threads, how Depression-era women turned feed sacks into fashion

spotlight.scarcityNote: Soup kitchens, bread lines and relief figures could not be sourced from pages we opened.
